text: A profitable company, under accrual accounting, can still run out of cash. That sounds contradictory, but you now have every piece needed to understand exactly why.

Recall accrual accounting: revenue is recorded when earned, expenses when incurred, not when cash moves. A business can report strong net income while accounts receivable keeps growing and cash keeps shrinking. Net income is an accrual-basis number; the cash flow statement translates that back into what actually happened to cash.

Every cash flow statement has three sections. Operating activities: cash from day-to-day business, starting from net income and adjusting for non-cash items and working capital changes. Investing activities: cash spent on or received from long-term assets. Financing activities: cash from or paid to owners and lenders.

Picture a fictional retailer, Pemberton Craft Supply, with ninety-two thousand in net income, but receivables grew thirty thousand and it bought fifty thousand of equipment financed by a twenty thousand loan. Operating activities net eighty thousand. Investing activities, negative fifty thousand. Financing activities, positive twenty thousand. Net increase in cash: fifty thousand - a different number from net income entirely.

A bank considering a loan cares less about paper profitability and more about whether a company generates enough operating cash to make its payments - exactly the gap this statement exposes. Up next, lesson twenty-eight: from transactions to financial statements.
